message.content:
Lions (Panthera leo) belong to the family **Felidae** in the order **Carnivora**, while zebras (Equus quagga) belong to the family **Equidae** in the order **Perissodactyla**.  
The two orders are part of the larger clade **Laurasiatheria** (which also contains groups such as Cetartiodactyla, Chiroptera, and others).  

**Thus, the most recent common ancestor of a lion and a zebra is the last common ancestor of the Laurasiatheria.**  
This ancestor was a small, probably insect‑eating mammal that lived roughly **70–80 million years ago** during the late Cretaceous to early Paleogene period. From that ancestor, the lineages that would become Carnivora and Perissodactyla diverged, eventually giving rise to the modern lion and zebra, respectively.
message.reasoning:
The user asks: "What is the common ancestor of lion and zebra?" They want a biological answer. The common ancestor of lion (Panthera leo) and zebra (Equus quagga) would be a common ancestor in the mammalian lineage. Both are mammals, but lions are felids (family Felidae), zebras are equids (family Equidae). They diverged from a common ancestor in the order Carnivora vs Perissodactyla? Actually lions are in order Carnivora, suborder Feliformia. Zebras are in order Perissodactyla (odd-toed ungulates). So their common ancestor would be a more distant mammalian ancestor, perhaps the last common ancestor of the clade that includes both Carnivora and Perissodactyla. That would be the last common ancestor of the Laurasiatheria? Actually Carnivora and Perissodactyla are both part of the clade Laurasiatheria. So the common ancestor would be the last common ancestor of Laurasiatheria, which is a mammalian ancestor that lived around 70-80 million years ago. But maybe the question expects "the common ancestor of lion and zebra is the last common ancestor of the mammalian clade Laurasiatheria, which lived about 70-80 million years ago." Or "the last common ancestor of the two species is the last common ancestor of the order Carnivora and Perissodactyla, which is a mammal that lived around 70-80 million years ago." Alternatively, they might want "the common ancestor is a mammal that lived in the late Cretaceous or early Paleogene." But maybe they want a specific taxonomic group: "the last common ancestor of the two species is the last common ancestor of the clade that includes both the Felidae and Equidae, which is the last common ancestor of the Laurasiatheria." So answer: "The last common ancestor of lions and zebras is the last common ancestor of the Laurasiatheria, a mammal that lived about 70-80 million years ago." Or "the last common ancestor of the two species is the last common ancestor of the order Carnivora and the order Perissodactyla, which is a mammal that lived around 70-80 million years ago."
